source.title: Adaptively Sampling-Reusing-Mixing Decomposed Gradients to Speed Up Sharpness Aware Minimization

record.file_problem: None; the supplied text contains the full paper.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses SAM’s claimed generalization benefit as motivation for an acceleration method, then reports ARSAM’s and baseline methods’ test performance. It does not test the listed versions about memorization, width, architecture, optimizer comparisons, batch size, dropout, sharpness measures, or memorized-example removal.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracy for SAM, ARSAM, SGD, and other methods, including under label noise. These results concern generalization performance but do not test a listed claim version. Comparisons to methods whose results are explicitly sourced from earlier papers are cited results, not this study’s own measurements.
record.test_reason: The study uses the sharpness–generalization connection to develop an acceleration method and evaluates its accuracy and speed. It does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness, correlate it with generalization gaps, or compare generalization measures as V7 requires. Its other experiments do not test V1–V6 or V8: label corruption lacks random-label fitting measurements, batch size is not varied within workloads, and Adam-based pose experiments do not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that ARSAM preserves approximately SAM-level generalization performance while accelerating training, sometimes achieving higher accuracy. They suggest that gradient reuse might find flatter regions but leave the explanation for future work.
record.recipe_differences: ARSAM adaptively samples and reuses decomposed PSF gradients to accelerate SAM; the study evaluates this new optimization method rather than reproducing a listed version’s recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different outcomes across dataset, architecture, label-noise rate, and α settings; accuracy and sampling frequency change with α in Table 1.

fits_no_version.finding: Across six CIFAR architecture–dataset combinations, ARSAM accuracy is 0.07–0.39 percentage points below SAM and exceeds SGD. Table 3 reports throughput of 134–146% of SAM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive reuse of decomposed SAM gradients can preserve approximately SAM-level classification accuracy while increasing training throughput.

fits_no_version.finding: At every reported symmetric label-noise rate on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, ARSAM test accuracy exceeds both SGD and SAM. These experiments do not report fitting the corrupted training labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ARSAM improves test accuracy over SGD and SAM under the tested symmetric label-noise conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: On Tiny-ImageNet, ARSAM accuracy exceeds SAM by 0.23 percentage points for ResNet-18 and 0.80 points for MobileNet.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ARSAM can match or improve SAM's test accuracy on the tested Tiny-ImageNet classifiers.

record.problems: The paper reports test accuracy but not training accuracy or the train-test generalization gap. It states that the main CIFAR experiments were repeated three times and reports averages and standard deviations; the label-noise table gives no uncertainty values.
record.rows_left_out: The study reports additional method comparisons in Tables 2–4, 7–8 and Table 3's non-SAM optimization baselines and variants. They are omitted because this extraction prioritizes SAM/ARSAM test-accuracy evidence relevant to the catalog claim; the additional tasks are segmentation, pose estimation, and quantization rather than the listed versions.

untested.parts: Coexistence of near-perfect fixed-random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same recipe; chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD-based optimization under limited or broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, and optimizer switching.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipes that compensate for batch size.
Dropout ablations, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus generalization gaps at similarly low training loss, including ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All rows measure optimizer performance outside the listed versions; cannot_determine does not imply an absent effect. The absence of training accuracy is not itself grounds to exclude test-accuracy evidence from every version, but it prevents these results from establishing V1's fitting comparison or V7's gap relationship. Gradient norms, PSF ratios, and convergence bounds do not supply the magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization comparison required by V7. E3's approximately 70% accuracy statement applies to CIFAR-10; CIFAR-100 at 80% noise yields 9.82% for SAM and 19.18% for ARSAM.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural versus random labels.
Test-error behavior when width exceeds the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer comparisons under the specified tuning regimes.
Large versus small batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurements and their association with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.
